newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--US May retail sales seen rising modestly.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--US May retail sales seen rising modestly.

text.p: U.S. retail sales are seen up modestly in May, boosted by an uptick in auto sales and some improvement in the general merchandise and the apparel store categories, Wall Street analysts said.
"I think we're going to see an increase in retail sales ... (but) I think it is going to be a very subdued number," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.

"We have a few things that are going to hold the number down. First, we had an increase in car sales in May, but it was a small one. We also had a rebound in general merchandise sales, but again not a very significant rebound," Low added.

In a Reuters poll, analysts forecast overall retail sales would rise 0.4 percent in May against a 0.3 percent decline in the previous month. The ex-auto indicator is seen up 0.3 percent in May against a 0.1 percent drop in the prior month.
The Commerce Department will release its retail sales report at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Thursday, June 12.
Analysts said auto sales were expected to rebound in May following the sector's weak performance in April.
"Given that the overall auto category has been weak recently, I just think it's due for a bit of a bounce back in May," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
In the non-auto category, experts said weekly indexes of retail activity showed modest increases during May, which suggest the overall retail sales is likely to be tame.
Digging into the details of the non-auto components, pundits said general merchandise and apparel stores are likely to be among the best performers in May.

"I think general merchandise and apparel will see some bounceback from a very slow performance in April. I don't mean to say sales were strong in May, but I think they were better than the reading we had in April and that should translate to modest month-to-month growth," Moran said.
The retail sales report has gained special importance recently since overall demand is seen by Wall Street as a key element for the Federal Reserve to determine monetary policy.
"It's going to be a very important number, specially since the Fed ... has suggested it is following final demand as a key determinant of monetary policy," Moran said.

If the overall retail numbers come in line with expectations, Wall Street analysts said the Fed might have a case to leave monetary policy unchanged once again during its next meeting on July 1 and July 2.

"If numbers come in line with forecasts, I think they would argue ... in favor of no Fed policy change in July because it would continue to indicate that consumer demand did slow in the second quarter," said Dana Saporta, economist at Stone and McCarthy Research Associates Inc.
Saporta is expecting overall retail sales to be up 0.3 percent in May, with the ex-autos component rising 0.2 percent.

"Retail sales will be possibly the most important indicator this week because the employment report last Friday sent mixed signals to the market and didn't provide a clear policy prescription for the Fed," she said.
May non-farm payrolls grew by 138,000 jobs against a revised 323,000 jump in the previous month. Meanwhile, the unemployment rate dropped to 4.8 percent in May from 4.9 percent in April.
The Fed last tightened monetary policy on March 25, when it boosted its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.
The Fed left rates unchanged during the latest meeting of its policy setting body on May 20.
